region.europe.label: Europe
region.europe.note.1: Monaco, San Marino, Vatican City and Liechtenstein have no column. Where the source records them, those records are not placed in a neighbouring country’s column either.
region.europe.note.2: Russia is split at 60°E: the western part is here, the rest is in Asia.
region.americas.label: Americas
region.americas.chartNote: Empty columns before 1500 mean no state is recorded, not empty land. Dashed blocks are states added from Wikidata whose territory is not mapped.
region.americas.note.1: Cliopatria maps few polities in the Americas before 1500. It includes the Olmec, Zapotec, Maya city-states, Teotihuacan, Classic Veracruz, Toltec, Michoacán, the Aztec Triple Alliance, Chimú, the Inca, the Chaco and Aztec Pueblo systems and the Haudenosaunee.
region.americas.note.2: Cliopatria does not map the Caral–Supe civilization, Chavín, Moche, Nazca, Wari, Tiwanaku, the Muisca Confederations or the Mississippian culture. They are added from Wikidata with its dates and shown in one country each, as dashed blocks without a mapped territory.
region.americas.note.3: Most Indigenous nations are still absent: neither source records them as states with dates and a place.
region.americas.note.4: The island states and territories of the Lesser Antilles share one column, as small Pacific islands do in Oceania. Hover its name to see which islands it includes.
region.oceania.label: Oceania
region.oceania.chartNote: The map source has almost no Pacific states before European contact. Dashed blocks (Tonga, Tahiti, Samoa, Pohnpei) are added from Wikidata; their territory is not mapped.
region.oceania.note.1: Cliopatria’s only Pacific state before colonisation is the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi (from 1791). The Tuʻi Tonga Empire, the Saudeleur dynasty of Pohnpei, the Kingdoms of Tahiti, Samoa and Tonga, and the later states of Samoa, Tonga and French Polynesia are added from Wikidata, without a mapped territory.
region.oceania.note.2: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations and Māori iwi are not shown: they are peoples and nations rather than states with dated borders in either source.
region.oceania.note.3: Small island states in Micronesia share one column so it covers at least about 1,000 km², as in the other regions. Hover its name to see which islands it includes. Tonga and the smaller Polynesian islands are combined the same way.
region.oceania.note.4: British settlement in Australia began in 1788 with the First Fleet. It appears here from 1828, when the source maps first show Britain holding more than 100,000 km² of today’s Australia.
region.africa-middle-east.label: Africa & Middle East
region.africa-middle-east.all: All of Africa & the Middle East
region.africa-middle-east.chartNote: Empty columns mean no state is recorded, not empty land. Dashed blocks are kingdoms added from Wikidata whose territory is not mapped.
region.africa-middle-east.note.1: Pre-colonial African states in the data include Kush, Axum, Makuria, Alodia, the Ghana Empire, Takrur, Kanem and Bornu, Mali, Songhai, Kongo, Oyo, Ashanti, Lunda, Merina, Sokoto, Zululand, the Ethiopian Empire, Adal, Funj, Darfur and Wadai.
region.africa-middle-east.note.2: Cliopatria does not map Kerma, the Garamantes, Ife, Benin, Kilwa, Great Zimbabwe, the Hausa and Mossi kingdoms, Jolof, Rwanda, Buganda, Mutapa, Ndongo, Luba, Bunyoro, Dahomey, Kuba or Kaabu. They are added from Wikidata (or a quoted Wikipedia article where Wikidata has no date) and shown in one country each, as dashed blocks without a mapped territory.
region.africa-middle-east.note.3: Columns follow Natural Earth’s country polygons: Palestine and Western Sahara are separate columns, Somaliland is counted within Somalia and Northern Cyprus within Cyprus. This is a mapping convention, not a position on disputed borders.
region.africa-middle-east.note.4: Turkey and Cyprus also appear in Europe, with identical data in both regions.
region.asia.label: Asia
region.asia.chartNote: Russia is split at 60°E: its western part is in Europe. Hong Kong and Macau are part of the China column.
region.asia.note.1: Coverage is dense from the Indus Valley Civilisation (from 3000 BCE in today’s Pakistan) and the Shang dynasty in China (from 1600 BCE). The source starts Japan with the Asuka period (540) and the Philippines with Namayan (1202), so earlier centuries there show no state.
region.asia.note.2: Columns follow Natural Earth’s country polygons: Taiwan is a separate column, Hong Kong and Macau are counted within China, Kashmir is divided as in those polygons and the Siachen Glacier has no column. This is a mapping convention, not a position on disputed borders.
region.asia.note.3: Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan are in this region; the Middle East, Iran and Turkey are in Africa & Middle East.

sources.periodNote: Period names on the time axis:
sources.noState: the source has no state there in any year.
sources.erasIntro: The Eras level shows the periods of each culture area from a cited periodization. Elsewhere, after an area’s last period and, where its source starts late, before its first one, it uses the region’s period bins per group of countries, only where the data records a state or culture. The names under each era are the cultures its source lists, when the chart has them, or else the records most present in the data.
sources.eraRevision: (English Wikipedia, revision read on the snapshot date).
sources.culturesIntro: {n} archaeological cultures and peoples come from Wikipedia’s lists of pre-Columbian cultures, North American archaeological periods and the periodization of pre-Columbian Peru. Each keeps the rows that list it, linked to the revision that was read. They are drawn like added states: pale, with a dashed edge.
sources.undated: Left out, no start or end date: {list}.
sources.addedIntro: The map source does not include these states, so they are added with their Wikidata dates (or a quoted Wikipedia article where Wikidata has none) and shown in one country without a mapped territory.
sources.eventsNote: {n} key events: Wikidata items classed as a battle, siege, invasion, campaign, war, revolution, rebellion, coup, treaty or pandemic{minLinks, select, none {} other {, with Wikipedia articles in at least {minLinks} languages}}. Each is placed by its own coordinates, else by its recorded locations, else by its country, and left out when those span more than {maxLanes} countries (the world wars, for example). Treaties sit where they were signed.
sources.linkNote: Wikidata links of the source’s states: {ok} confirmed by matching dates, {unknown} without dates to compare, {corrected} corrected through the Wikipedia article, {mismatch} hidden because their dates do not match the state. Wikidata’s dates are shown beside the chart’s in each state’s story; the chart keeps the map source’s years.
sources.storiesNote: Each story’s summary and lead image are read from Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons when you open it, in your language where an article exists. The text is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; each image carries its own author and licence in its caption. The revision read is linked under the story’s sources.
sources.read.1: Each column is a country with today’s borders. Each block is a state that held part of it.
sources.read.2: Darker blocks held more of the country. Hatched blocks count the state together with its vassals.
sources.read.3: Select any block, era or event to open its story on the right. Select another to change the story; the country you picked from stays in view.
sources.read.4: Where too many small states would sit side by side, they are gathered into one “+” block. Select it to list them.
sources.read.5: The time axis is compressed before 500 CE so recent centuries have more room. Drag, scroll or pinch to move and zoom. Zooming in widens the countries too, around your fingers, so the stacked blocks of a country can be read and selected.
sources.read.6: Start and end years follow the source maps and can be a few years off the usual textbook dates.
sources.read.unmapped: Pale blocks with a dashed edge are states the map source does not cover; their territory is not mapped.
sources.read.events: Dots are key events; a rail below a dot runs to the event’s last year. Zoom in to see more of them.
